prize_parts.citation: for the optical lattice clock: magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms, which brought atomic clocks to the 10^-18 level of accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: After reading the full set of opening ballots I move the optical lattice clock to the top of my own list, ahead of circuit QED, which I ranked first. The case rests on what the shortlist evidence shows. Five of eight members ranked B045 and four of them placed it in the top three or as a clearly strong candidate, the broadest base of any shortlisted item, and the reasons given by Kroll, Lindroth and Pearce are scientific and not tactical. Katori's magic-wavelength idea removed the trade-off between many-atom statistics and motional/Stark shifts, and Ye's group turned it into a controlled many-body system with fractional uncertainty near 1e-18, mm-scale gravitational redshift measurements and bounds on drifts of constants. This is a clean experiment that makes a basic effect visible and controllable. It has been reproduced and surpassed in many national laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, SYRTE, PTB, NIST), with routine inter-laboratory comparisons, and the attribution is a tidy two-person configuration that all five supporters agree on. It is mature and robust, which is exactly the standard I try to apply to discoveries in my own field.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that precision-timekeeping has been rewarded repeatedly (Ramsey 1989, Hall and Hansch 2005, Wineland and Haroche 2012), so the committee must be able to state what is new in the citation and not just a better number. Ion clocks and the frequency comb are the earlier layers on which lattice clocks stand, and a critic can argue that the lattice clock is an engineering refinement of established atomic-physics tools, with its main payoffs (redefinition of the second, geodesy, dark-matter searches) still prospective. Also, a prize here leaves out Hall-type, Ludlow and Lemonde-type contributions, and the Ye group's own many-body clock work is a later layer than the magic-wavelength concept. I also hold that circuit QED has the stronger claim of opening a new regime of light-matter interaction, so my preference for B045 is partly a judgement on timing and robustness.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the optical lattice clock first as a measurement breakthrough combining Doppler- and recoil-free interrogation with many-atom statistics, with reproduction across independent laboratories and a clean Katori-Ye attribution.
responses.response: I agree with the core of this and it moved me. Where I would qualify is the framing as 'measurement' only: the importance of the lattice clock is that it is a controllable quantum many-body system, and the prize citation should say the magic-wavelength trapping is the discovery, not the 1e-18 number, so that it is distinguishable from the 2005 and 2012 prizes. I also note that Kroll ranks circuit QED second, and we agree that cQED is a serious but later candidate.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube's astrophysical neutrinos first, valuing a detector-driven discovery that opened a new observational window, with Halzen and Karle credited, and ranks the lattice clock second.
responses.response: I respect the argument that IceCube is a genuine new window and I defer to Pearce and Danielsson on astroparticle matters. My hesitation is that the supplied attribution is not settled: Pearce himself notes AMANDA leaders and key analysts, and the source identifications (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) are less independently confirmed by other experiments. The diffuse flux is solid, but only two members support it, whereas the clock has independent confirmation from many laboratories and a cleaner credit. If the committee can settle the credit question I would not oppose B016.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks topological insulators first as a general mechanism, a topological invariant protecting edge states, that reshaped how condensed-matter phases are classified, with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as core names.
responses.response: The conceptual weight of the Z2 classification is real and outside my own expertise, so I defer on the physics. My concern is practical: the shortlist entry credits four names, and Mehlig and Olsson themselves propose different trios (Mele versus Hasan), which suggests the attribution is genuinely contested and may be hard to resolve to three. I would want that settled before I consider B040 ahead of a candidate whose credit is not in doubt.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks quantum control of mechanical motion first as a fundamental advance about the quantum-classical boundary, with stable interpretation across platforms, and the lattice clock second.
responses.response: I find her fundamental framing attractive and I ranked B008 myself, but I must be honest about the attribution: five credited names for a three-person limit, and Lindroth's trio differs from the Aspelmeyer, Kippenberg, Teufel trio that Kroll and I proposed. That leaves out Cleland and Painter, who made decisive demonstrations. Until that is resolved I cannot make it my preferred configuration, though we agree on the clock as a strong second choice.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first as a prediction by Bistritzer and MacDonald followed by the Jarillo-Herrero experiment, creating the moire quantum materials field.
responses.response: It is a clean prediction-plus-experiment story and the field is clearly important. But three other members, Danielsson, Olsson and Pearce, place it at rank 7 and Mehlig at 3, and the credits omit Cao, Dean and Young. The mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated, so on maturity I would wait. That is a timing judgement and not a judgement on its quality, and I would expect it to return.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as a distinct achievement after the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes, or as a refinement of them.

Whether circuit QED should be held back because of the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits, and whether the architects (Blais, Wallraff, Schoelkopf) without Girvin and Huang would be accepted as the right credit.
Whether Hall, Lemonde, Ludlow or other lattice-clock contributors would be seen as omitted by a Katori and Ye prize.
I have not been able to judge the astroparticle and topological-matter cases in depth and rely on colleagues for those.
statement.conflict_note: I ranked circuit QED first in my opening ballot. As director of WACQT and a theorist in superconducting circuits at Chalmers, I have a close professional connection to that field, and Chalmers colleagues work with groups near it, so I should recuse myself from deciding on B026 (and likely B008, which overlaps with circuit devices). No specific personal connection to the lattice-clock candidates Katori and Ye is apparent from the provided profile.
